title: Physical Atari: A Robust and Accessible Platform for Real-time Reinforcement Learning on Robots
summary: We built a robot called the Robotroller that actuates an Atari CX40+ controller and a device called the Atari Devbox that renders the game frame and the reward signal from the Arcade Learning Environment on a screen. The Robotroller and the Atari Devbox, together with an off-the-shelf camera and a desktop computer, constitute a system that can be used to study reinforcement learning algorithms in the physical world. We call the full system Physical Atari. In this paper, we detail the key decisions that make Physical Atari a robust and accessible platform. To make the system robust, we designed the Robotroller so that all movement is done through bearings, which reduces wear. Additionally, we wrote software that monitors the state of the servos at a high frequency and intervenes to limit stress. To make the system accessible, we used affordable off-the-shelf components and parts that can be manufactured using consumer 3D printers. Physical Atari can be built for under $1,000 and has been used for weeks of non-stop reinforcement learning experiments without any mechanical failures. We used it to validate that reinforcement learning algorithms can learn directly on robots and show that even small distribution shifts between learning and deployment can significantly degrade the performance of policies. Our results underscore the importance of on-device adaptation for strong performance on robots.

AI.tldr: The authors built Physical Atari, a $1,000 robot platform that interfaces an Atari controller with an Atari Devbox for reinforcement learning experiments, demonstrating that RL can learn on physical robots but is sensitive to distribution shifts between learning and deployment.
AI.motivation: To create a robust and accessible platform for studying reinforcement learning algorithms in the physical world, specifically by enabling direct interaction with Atari games through physical hardware.
AI.method: They built Robotroller (actuates Atari CX40+ controller) and Atari Devbox (renders game frames/rewards), combined with camera and computer. Key design: all movement via bearings to reduce wear, servo monitoring software to limit stress. Used affordable off-the-shelf components and 3D printable parts.
AI.result: Physical Atari can be built for under $1,000 and runs for weeks without mechanical failures. Validated that RL algorithms can learn directly on robots. Showed that even small distribution shifts between learning and deployment significantly degrade policy performance.
AI.conclusion: Results underscore the importance of on-device adaptation for achieving strong performance on robots, as distribution shifts between training and deployment environments can substantially impact policy effectiveness.

title: Mesh Inference: A Formal Model of Collective Intelligence Without a Center
summary: We present a formal model of mesh inference: how a population of independent agents, each holding private state and exchanging only admitted, typed observations, derives a conclusion none of them holds alone, with no central coordinator and no agent exposed. No agent shares weights, gradients, or hidden state, and the agents may span different teams, networks, and organizations. Motivated by the observation that asking a model is energy-minimizing inference, we model the mesh as a coupled free energy that each agent relaxes locally. We show that a single admission/emission policy governs three properties. First, mesh inference converges to a unique answer for any admission, symmetric or not, because the coupling is always an M-matrix. Second, it is identification-complete: it derives the centralized optimum exactly when the contributing views are carrier-connected. Third, it is observation-only: no node transmits its internals, and confidentiality is the dual of identification. Content-addressed lineage is the only global side-channel. In the linear-Gaussian regime every derived answer is determined, hence equal to the centralized optimum, at O(diam^2) latency, the measured price of removing the center. One such derivation is one turn of a center-free learning loop, which we formalize as architecture rather than prove. The open problem we state is when asking improves the collective rather than corrupting it: whether the non-linear closure derives an upgraded answer or a confident error. To our knowledge, this is the first formal model of mesh inference.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first formal model of mesh inference—decentralized inference where independent agents with private state exchange typed observations to derive a conclusion none holds alone, without a central coordinator. The model treats mesh inference as a coupled free energy minimization problem governed by a single admission/emission policy, which ensures convergence to a unique answer (M-matrix property), identification-complete performance (derives centralized optimum when views are carrier-connected), and observation-only execution (confidentiality is dual to identification).
AI.motivation: The authors observe that "asking a model" is energy-minimizing inference and want to formalize how a population of independent agents can derive a conclusion none holds alone without a central coordinator or exposed agents—motivated by the need for decentralized, privacy-preserving inference across teams and organizations.
AI.method: The model represents mesh inference as a coupled free energy that each agent relaxes locally, governed by a single admission/emission policy. The coupling structure is proven to be an M-matrix, which ensures convergence properties. Content-addressed lineage is the only global side-channel. The framework is analyzed in both the linear-Gaussian regime (where every derived answer equals the centralized optimum at O(diam²) latency) and for open problems regarding non-linear closure.
AI.result: The model proves that a single admission/emission policy guarantees: (1) convergence to a unique answer for any admission policy (symmetric or not), (2) identification-complete performance (derives the centralized optimum exactly when contributing views are carrier-connected), and (3) observation-only execution (no node transmits internals, with confidentiality being the dual of identification). In the linear-Gaussian regime, every derived answer equals the centralized optimum at O(diam²) latency.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes mesh inference as a formally defined concept and demonstrates that it can achieve centralized-optimal performance with O(diam²) latency while maintaining confidentiality. The open problem is determining whether asking (non-linear closure) improves the collective or corrupts it—this remains an open question for future work.

title: WorkBenchMark: A LEGO-Based Assembly Benchmark with an Assembly-by-Disassembly Baseline for the Smart Manufacturing League
summary: We introduceWorkBenchMark, a LEGO Duplo-based robotic assembly benchmark motivated by the RoboCup Smart Manufacturing League. Robotic assembly couples low-level manipulation with task-level symbolic reasoning under physical constraints, a combination that current end-to-end learning methods do not yet solve reliably. The benchmark provides 400 tasks across four complexity tiers. We provide an open-vocabulary perception, Assembly-by-Disassembly baseline solution. Our planning-based pipeline outperforms a modern vision-language-action approach across all tiers. The benchmark, simulation environment, and baseline implementation will be released openly to support the broader robotic assembly community.

AI.tldr: WorkBenchMark introduces a LEGO Duplo-based robotic assembly benchmark with 400 tasks across four complexity tiers. It provides an open-vocabulary perception and Assembly-by-Disassembly baseline solution that outperforms modern vision-language-action approaches across all tiers.
AI.motivation: Robotic assembly combines low-level manipulation with task-level symbolic reasoning under physical constraints, a combination that current end-to-end learning methods do not solve reliably. This work is motivated by the RoboCup Smart Manufacturing League.
AI.method: The benchmark provides 400 tasks across four complexity tiers. The authors implemented an open-vocabulary perception system and an Assembly-by-Disassembly baseline solution. They compared a planning-based pipeline against a modern vision-language-action approach.
AI.result: The planning-based pipeline outperforms the modern vision-language-action approach across all complexity tiers.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark, simulation environment, and baseline implementation will be released openly to support the broader robotic assembly community.

title: SIGMA: Skill-Incidence Graphs for Compositional Multi-Agent Design
summary: Existing graph-based multi-agent system (MAS) designers mainly improve collaboration by optimizing communication topologies over predefined agents, roles, or groups. However, because each node remains a closed-set entity, these methods struggle to generalize to tasks that require unseen combinations of capabilities. We propose SIGMA, a skill-incidence graph framework that constructs agents as task-conditioned bundles of reusable skills. Given a task and a skill library, SIGMA predicts a skill-agent incidence matrix, composes agent node embeddings from selected skills, and decodes a communication topology over the constructed agents. During execution, skill-specific mailboxes route messages to the relevant assigned capabilities, making the incidence structure directly operational. Across six reasoning and coding benchmarks with three base LLMs, SIGMA achieves the best average performance and improves over CARD, the strongest non-compositional topology-based baseline, by 2.06, 2.36, and 1.75 points, respectively. It also shows stronger robustness to unseen skill libraries, with an average performance drop of only 0.96 points. These results suggest that compositional node construction is a complementary and important axis for multi-agent design beyond communication topology optimization. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SIGMA-2338/.

AI.tldr: SIGMA is a skill-incidence graph framework that constructs agents as task-conditioned bundles of reusable skills, enabling better generalization to unseen task combinations through compositional node construction.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based multi-agent system (MAS) designers optimize communication topologies over predefined agents, roles, or groups. However, because each node remains a closed-set entity, these methods struggle to generalize to tasks requiring unseen combinations of capabilities.
AI.method: SIGMA constructs agents as task-conditioned bundles of reusable skills. Given a task and a skill library, it predicts a skill-agent incidence matrix, composes agent node embeddings from selected skills, and decodes a communication topology. During execution, skill-specific mailboxes route messages to relevant assigned capabilities.
AI.result: Across six reasoning and coding benchmarks with three base LLMs, SIGMA achieves the best average performance and improves over CARD (the strongest non-compositional topology-based baseline) by 2.06, 2.36, and 1.75 points respectively. It also shows stronger robustness to unseen skill libraries, with an average performance drop of only 0.96 points.
AI.conclusion: Compositional node construction is a complementary and important axis for multi-agent design beyond communication topology optimization.

title: 3D Scene Graphs: Open Challenges and Future Directions
comment: Invited article for the Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems Volume 10
summary: 3D Scene Graphs (3DSGs) have emerged as a powerful representation for spatial AI by combining geometric grounding with semantic and relational abstractions of the environment. Their expressiveness has made them relevant to a broad range of problems in robotics and computer vision, including manipulation, navigation, task planning, scene understanding, and many others. However, the field remains fragmented: different communities adopt distinct formulations, construction pipelines, and evaluation protocols, making it difficult to compare methods, identify common assumptions, and assess remaining challenges for robust real-world deployment. This survey provides a unified and critical review of 3DSGs, with particular emphasis on open challenges and future directions. We first formalize 3DSGs under a common definition and analyze the principal modeling choices that characterize existing formulations, including node and edge attributes, hierarchical structure, dynamic scene representations, and affordance-aware extensions. We then review how 3DSGs are built from raw sensory observations, discussing the most common terminologies, conventions, and techniques. Finally, we examine downstream applications and evaluation strategies, from intrinsic graph quality to task-level performance. To support the community, we also provide a dedicated website that organizes and extends the surveyed content, accessible at https://3dscenegraphs.com/.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey paper providing a unified review of 3D Scene Graphs (3DSGs) across robotics and computer vision, covering definitions, construction methods, applications, and evaluation strategies, along with an online resource.
AI.motivation: The field of 3DSGs is fragmented with different communities adopting distinct formulations, construction pipelines, and evaluation protocols, making it difficult to compare methods, identify common assumptions, and assess challenges for real-world deployment.
AI.method: The survey formalizes 3DSGs under a common definition, analyzes principal modeling choices (node/edge attributes, hierarchical structure, dynamic scene representations, affordance-aware extensions), reviews construction pipelines from raw sensory observations, and examines downstream applications and evaluation strategies. It also provides a dedicated website (https://3dscenegraphs.com/) to organize and extend the surveyed content.
AI.result: Provides a unified and critical review of 3DSGs that organizes and extends surveyed content online, offering a reference for understanding the field's current state.
AI.conclusion: The survey identifies open challenges and future directions for 3DSGs in applications such as manipulation, navigation, task planning, and scene understanding.

title: Blame is easier than praise: Measuring off-ball defensive performance in football
summary: The defensive performance of football players is commonly measured through a limited number of actions like tackles and interceptions while their continuous impact through positional behaviour has hardly been studied before. We formulate this problem as an attribution over multi-agent spatiotemporal trajectories without player-level ground truth labels, where event-level changes of expected threat are distributed among individuals. We propose a framework that performs this attribution using player involvement scores calculated from defensive pressure areas (DPAs). By computing role-conditioned baselines within automatically detected team structures, we can determine each defender's expected responsibility for threat created through arbitrary passes. The validity and robustness of this approach are evaluated on a uniquely extensive cross-gender and cross-competition data set, including positional and event data from 64 matches of the men's World Cup, 116 matches of the women's German Bundesliga and 336 matches of the men's German 3. Liga. In the absence of a ground truth, we propose an evaluation protocol that combines multiple relatively weak proxies into robust summary scores. We find a validity score that is improved by around 1 standard deviation compared to the best action-based metric and demonstrate that many popular measures show limited validity. The "blame" for conceding high-value actions shows especially strong correlations with external ratings and market values, making it the first published metric in football to reliably measure positioning errors. All code underlying this work is publicly available to support reproducibility and further research.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel framework for attributing defensive responsibilities in football (soccer) based on multi-agent spatiotemporal trajectories, using player involvement scores from defensive pressure areas (DPAs) to measure defensive positioning and performance without requiring ground truth labels.
AI.motivation: Football defensive performance is typically measured only through limited actions like tackles and interceptions, while continuous impact through positional behavior has been largely unstudied. The authors aim to develop a method that can attribute threat responsibility among defenders based on their positioning and defensive pressure.
AI.method: The authors formulate defensive attribution as a problem over multi-agent spatiotemporal trajectories without player-level ground truth. They propose a framework using player involvement scores calculated from defensive pressure areas (DPAs), combined with role-conditioned baselines within automatically detected team structures to determine each defender's expected responsibility for threat created through passes.
AI.result: The method was validated on an extensive dataset of 516 matches across men's World Cup, women's German Bundesliga, and men's German 3. Liga. The approach achieved a validity score improved by ~1 standard deviation compared to the best action-based metric, with strong correlations between "blame" metrics for conceding high-value actions and external ratings and market values.
AI.conclusion: This is the first published metric in football that reliably measures positioning errors. The proposed framework provides a more comprehensive view of defensive performance than traditional action-based metrics, and the all code is publicly available for reproducibility and further research.

title: DiffusionVS: A Generative Framework for Robust Visual Servoing Based on Diffusion Policy
summary:
Visual servoing is a fundamental technique in robotic manipulation and navigation. Regression-based visual servoing frequently experiences trajectory jitter as a result of noise-sensitive single-step mappings and the accumulation of errors during distribution shifts. In contrast, Diffusion Policy maintains temporal consistency by predicting action sequences and improves robustness through implicit data augmentation.
  This paper presents a novel diffusion-based servoing method. Based on Diffusion Policy, the proposed approach uses normalized image coordinates of observed tag corners as input and generates camera velocity through conditional denoising. To overcome the generalization limitations of models trained on static datasets, an online training paradigm is adopted, continuously expanding the diversity of training data through interactive experience collection. This strategy substantially enhances both the performance and generalization capability of the model. Comprehensive simulations and real-world experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving success rates of nearly 100\% in simulation and 93\% in physical experiments. Beyond the specific pipeline, we further validate the generality of the diffusion mechanism. Experiments show that existing visual servoing networks consistently achieve improved performance when integrated with our diffusion-based module. These results indicate that the proposed strategy possesses broad applicability and can enhance various visual servoing systems beyond the specific architecture presented here.

AI.tldr: A diffusion-based visual servoing method that uses normalized image coordinates of observed tag corners as input to generate camera velocity through conditional denoising, employing online training to overcome generalization limitations and achieving near-perfect success rates in both simulation and physical experiments.
AI.motivation: Regression-based visual servoing suffers from trajectory jitter due to noise-sensitive single-step mappings and error accumulation during distribution shifts, while Diffusion Policy maintains temporal consistency through action sequence prediction and improves robustness via implicit data augmentation.
AI.method: Based on Diffusion Policy, the proposed approach uses normalized image coordinates of observed tag corners as input and generates camera velocity through conditional denoising. To overcome generalization limitations of static dataset training, an online training paradigm is adopted that continuously expands training data diversity through interactive experience collection.
AI.result: Comprehensive simulations and real-world experiments demonstrate effectiveness, achieving success rates of nearly 100% in simulation and 93% in physical experiments. Additionally, experiments show existing visual servoing networks consistently achieve improved performance when integrated with the diffusion-based module.
AI.conclusion: The proposed strategy possesses broad applicability and can enhance various visual servoing systems beyond the specific architecture presented, validating the generality of the diffusion mechanism for visual servoing tasks.

title: Formal Verification of Learned Multi-Agent Communication Policies via Decision Tree Distillation
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026), Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA, September 27-October 1, 2026
summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables agents to develop coordination strategies through emergent communication, but neural policies lack the formal safety guarantees required for safety-critical robotic deployment in drone swarms and autonomous vehicle fleets. We present the first end-to-end framework for safety verification of learned multi-agent communication policies through policy abstraction: neural policies are distilled into interpretable decision trees, then formally verified, with empirical validation confirming that verified safety properties transfer to original networks. Our four-stage pipeline consists of domain-specific feature extraction from agent observations, decision tree distillation achieving 97.9% +/- 1.2% fidelity to neural policies, automated translation to PRISM probabilistic model checker specifications with complete feature-to-state-variable correspondence, and compositional verification of Probabilistic Computation Tree Logic (PCTL) properties via pairwise decomposition with union-bound aggregation and empirical neighbor modeling. Evaluating Vector-Quantized Variational Information Bottleneck (VQ-VIB) policies for multi-drone coordination with 5-7 agents, we verify 18 temporal logic properties across safety, liveness, and cooperation, achieving 88.9% property satisfaction with all five safety thresholds satisfied (0.3% collision probability vs. 1% threshold). Monte Carlo validation of original neural policies confirms that verified safety properties transfer with <=0.6 percentage-point deviation (95% CI). Discrete VQ-VIB messages provide +11.6 to +13.6 percentage-point fidelity advantages over continuous methods, enabling 3-4x faster verification. Our framework provides empirically validated safety verification for distilled policy abstractions, serving as a practical bridge between deep MARL and formal safety workflows for multi-robot deployment.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent reinforcement learning enables coordination through emergent communication but lacks formal safety guarantees for safety-critical robotic deployment. This paper presents an end-to-end framework that abstracts neural policies into decision trees, formally verifies them using PRISM's probabilistic model checker with PCTL properties, and empirically validates that verified safety properties transfer to original networks.
AI.motivation: Neural policies in MARL lack formal safety guarantees required for safety-critical robotic deployment in drone swarms and autonomous vehicle fleets. While MARL enables coordination through emergent communication, there's a gap between learned policies and the formal verification needed for real-world robotic applications.
AI.method: Four-stage pipeline: (1) domain-specific feature extraction from agent observations, (2) decision tree distillation achieving 97.9% ± 1.2% fidelity to neural policies, (3) automated translation to PRISM probabilistic model checker specifications with complete feature-to-state-variable correspondence, (4) compositional verification of PCTL properties via pairwise decomposition with union-bound aggregation and empirical neighbor modeling.
AI.result: Verified 18 temporal logic properties across safety, liveness, and cooperation for 5-7 agent multi-drone coordination using VQ-VIB policies, achieving 88.9% property satisfaction with all five safety thresholds satisfied (0.3% collision probability vs. 1% threshold). Monte Carlo validation confirms verified safety properties transfer with ≤0.6 percentage-point deviation (95% CI). Discrete VQ-VIB messages provide +11.6 to +13.6 percentage-point fidelity advantages over continuous methods, enabling 3-4x faster verification.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides empirically validated safety verification for distilled policy abstractions, serving as a practical bridge between deep MARL and formal safety workflows for multi-robot deployment, addressing the critical safety gap in neural policies for safety-critical robotic applications.

title: Playful Agentic Robot Learning
summary: Current agentic robot systems can write executable Code-as-Policy programs, observe feedback, and revise behavior across multiple attempts, but they remain largely task-driven: reusable skills are acquired only after explicit instructions. We study Playful Agentic Robot Learning, where an embodied coding agent uses self-directed play as a continual skill-learning stage before downstream tasks arrive. We introduce RATs, Robotics Agent Teams designed for play-time skill acquisition. During play, RATs proposes novel yet learnable exploratory tasks, plans and executes robot-code policies, verifies intermediate progress, diagnoses failures, retries with dense, step-level feedback, and distills successful executions into a persistent code skill library. At test time, the agent reuses relevant skills from this frozen library to help solve new tasks. Experiments in LIBERO-PRO and MolmoSpaces show that play-learned skills improve held-out downstream tasks over no-play and random-play baselines, with 20.6 and 17.0 percentage-point gains over CaP-Agent0 on LIBERO-PRO and MolmoSpaces, respectively. Moreover, the learned skills can be plugged into other inference-time Code-as-Policy agents by simply retrieving them into the context, improving RoboSuite and real-world transfer by 8.9 and 8.8 points, respectively, without finetuning the underlying model.

AI.tldr: Playful Agentic Robot Learning enables embodied coding agents to autonomously acquire reusable skills through self-directed play before tackling downstream tasks, using Robotics Agent Teams (RATs) that propose tasks, execute robot-code policies, verify progress, diagnose failures, and distill successful executions into a persistent code skill library.
AI.motivation: Current agentic robot systems are largely task-driven, meaning reusable skills require explicit instructions rather than being acquired autonomously through exploration. There is a need for a continual skill-learning stage where agents can develop reusable capabilities before specific tasks arrive.
AI.method: The researchers introduce Robotics Agent Teams (RATs), which use self-directed play as a continual skill-learning stage. During play, RATs propose novel yet learnable exploratory tasks, plan and execute robot-code policies, verify intermediate progress, diagnose failures, retry with dense step-level feedback, and distill successful executions into a persistent code skill library. At test time, agents retrieve relevant skills from this frozen library to solve new tasks.
AI.result: Experiments in LIBERO-PRO and MolmoSpaces show that play-learned skills improve held-out downstream tasks over no-play and random-play baselines, with 20.6 and 17.0 percentage-point gains over CaP-Agent0 respectively. Additionally, the learned skills can be plugged into other inference-time Code-as-Policy agents by simply retrieving them into the context, improving RoboSuite and real-world transfer by 8.9 and 8.8 points respectively without finetuning the underlying model.
AI.conclusion: Self-directed play enables embodied coding agents to autonomously acquire reusable skills that can be effectively transferred to downstream tasks and other agents, demonstrating that skill acquisition through exploration significantly outperforms task-driven approaches without requiring finetuning of the underlying model.

title: Deep-Unfolded Coordination
comment: The second and third authors contributed equally (equal second authorship). 35 pages (10 pages main text), 17 figures, 3 tables
summary: Distributed optimization is a highly scalable and structurally transparent technique to solve multi-agent robotics problems; however, such methods often suffer from the need for highly-specialized, problem-specific hyperparameter tunings. In this work, we propose Deep Coordinator, a deep-unfolding framework that learns to dynamically adjust the hyperparameters of ADMM-DDP, a popular distributed solver for robotics tasks, at solve-time in response to optimizer performance. Our architecture consists of unrolling a fixed number of ADMM-DDP iterations into a neural network with learnable functions between layers mapping the optimizer state to the next hyperparameters. To the best of our knowledge, Deep Coordinator is the first deep-unfolding framework to adapt the penalty parameters of a non-convex optimizer at solve-time; we show that the mainstream supervised approach can yield degenerate solutions when training such models, and propose an unsupervised learning scheme. On simulations with fleets of cars and quadrotors, Deep Coordinator produces trajectories of comparable quality 6.18-9.44x faster than conventional solvers. Furthermore, Deep Coordinator retains its performance benefits when deployed to systems up to 8x larger than trained on.

AI.tldr: Deep Coordinator is a deep-unfolding framework that learns to dynamically adjust ADMM-DDP hyperparameters at solve-time, using an unsupervised learning scheme to avoid degenerate solutions, achieving 6.18-9.44x speedup on multi-agent robotics tasks while maintaining performance at 8x larger scales than training.
AI.motivation: Distributed optimization methods for multi-agent robotics are scalable and transparent but require highly-specialized, problem-specific hyperparameter tuning, which is labor-intensive and limits accessibility. The authors aim to automate this tuning process.
AI.method: Deep Coordinator unrolls ADMM-DDP iterations into a neural network with learnable functions mapping optimizer state to next hyperparameters. It adapts penalty parameters of a non-convex optimizer at solve-time. An unsupervised learning scheme is proposed because mainstream supervised approaches can yield degenerate solutions when training such models.
AI.result: On simulations with fleets of cars and quadrotors, Deep Coordinator produces trajectories of comparable quality to conventional solvers but 6.18-9.44x faster. It retains performance benefits when deployed to systems up to 8x larger than the training scale.
AI.conclusion: Deep Coordinator successfully automates hyperparameter tuning for distributed optimization, providing significant speedup without quality degradation and maintaining performance at scale, demonstrating the effectiveness of deep-unfolding for adaptive optimization solvers.

title: Simulating Robotic Locomotion in Sand: Resistive Force Theory in an Open-Source Physics Engine
summary: Recent advancements in Resistive Force Theory (RFT) enable approximation of ground reaction forces for locomotion in sand without the computational expense of modeling interactions with individual grains. However, these tools have been absent in 3D physics engines commonly used for robot simulation. We explore if resistive force approximations are sufficient, when integrated with standard dynamics calculations, to provide a stable substrate for a freely walking robot. To determine this, we implement 3D Granular Resistive Force Theory (3D RFT) in a physics simulation engine, MuJoCo. We verify simulations in multiple scenarios to demonstrate that key trends due to end effector shape, speed, and loading are preserved. Our implementation predicts walking distance and foot sinkage of a 12-Degree of Freedom hexapod robot within 20\% of experiments in sand. While RFT has inherent approximations, the open source tool described here has potential to help develop new and improved robot designs to traverse granular media substrates.

This paper implements 3D Granular Resistive Force Theory (3D RFT) in the MuJoCo physics engine and demonstrates that it can provide a stable substrate for freely walking robots, with predictions within 20% of experimental data.

However, these tools have been absent in 3D physics engines commonly used for robot simulation. The authors explore if resistive force approximations, when integrated with standard dynamics calculations, are sufficient to provide a stable substrate for a freely walking robot.
